thread.title: Dusty May credits Vlad Goldin, Danny Wolf for this year's frontcourt 'dogs'
thread.title_full: Dusty May credits Vlad Goldin, Danny Wolf for this year's frontcourt 'dogs'

author: Drew Lenard
title: Dusty May credits Vlad Goldin, Danny Wolf for this year's frontcourt 'dogs'
text:
Dusty May learned two big things from last year’s back-to-back defeats at the hands of then-No.7 Michigan State.
The first was the importance of keeping composure and poise in a rivalry where emotions almost always run high, and playing nothing but 40 minutes of controlled basketball. The second lesson was harder to swallow.
“The other thing was our personnel last year, we didn’t have enough dog to win the league,” the No. 2 Michigan men’s basketball team coach said Monday. “We had some, and I love our guys from last year, but we just didn’t have enough dog.”
As point-blank as it gets. May knew what he was lacking, and he went out and got it in the offseason, pulling in all three of his current frontcourt bruisers within 11 days of each other. Graduate forward Yaxel Lendeborg, sophomore forward Morez Johnson Jr. and junior center Aday Mara are the founding fathers of the nation’s scariest interior defense, and play a major role in the Wolverines’ offensive production as well.
That was all on full display Friday night against the Spartans. The trio combined for 46 points from all parts of the court while keeping an interior-focused Michigan State offense out of the paint with their daunting defensive presence. And as a result, Michigan secured its first win at Breslin Center in eight years.
May’s three ‘dogs’ down low have proven time and time again this season they can coexist, despite what much of the offseason noise initially declared. No matter how many members of the media and opposing coaching staff warned May that the three big talents would overcrowd the frontcourt, fight each other for playing time and take turns playing hero ball, he didn’t listen. Neither did Lendeborg, Johnson or Mara — because they’d all seen it work before.
“I think they all bought in because of the vision our team played with last year, as far as outside-the-box-thinking, and Danny (Wolf) and Vlad (Goldin) did a lot of that,” May said. “They did something you don’t see from two seven footers. They were out there playing jazz together.”
Wolf and Goldin, who have both since made their way onto NBA rosters, certainly had a unique rhythm on the court together at Michigan. May had the two giants running the pick-and-roll together, allowing Wolf to play into his strengths as both an exterior shooter and elite passer, and Goldin to roll hard for the rim for easy looks under the basket. The Wolverines may have lacked in the ‘dog’ department last year, but there was no denying Wolf and Goldin that moniker.
Prior to playing for the Wolverines, Goldin was a leader on the FAU squad that made a push to the 2023 Final Four, and Wolf was a highly touted transfer known for being the definition of a stretch big. In other words, they had both already established themselves separately, but they’re in the league because of how May utilized them together.
May had the same vision this year when recruiting his freshly oversized frontcourt, and he’s largely succeeded in bringing it to life. Lendeborg was already a star before arriving at Michigan, but he has supported Johnson and Mara having their own breakout seasons alongside him. They take turns in the driver’s seat depending on the opponent and their matchups. That’s exactly what May preaches, but it’s up to the athletes to put his plan into action.
“Their personality traits allow them to (compete with each other), but also respect each other,” May said. “If you want to win big, you don’t go where there aren’t any good players. … You don’t have to put up big numbers, you just have to be efficient and win.”
May has more ‘dogs’ this year, but that wouldn’t be possible without the two who left the kennel in the offseason.
Without Goldin and Wolf paving the way for what a loaded frontcourt can do under May’s supervision, it’s not as likely the current group gets together in Ann Arbor. And it’s not as likely the Wolverines walk out of Breslin Center with a win and the No. 2 national ranking.
